> **2026-10-23 [MAJOR: the `.ifs` concatenation idea is disproven and the RESOURCE LAYER IS NOW SETTLED - but the client still stalls at ui_state 5]**
> **The `.ifs` finding** (from an independent investigative run, see `docs/IFS-MERGE-RESULT.md`): `.ifs` is a **container** of *complete signed fastfiles*, not a fragment stream. **A legal fastfile length is always `0x115 + N*0x2000`**, and concatenating k members yields `size mod 0x2000 = (277k) mod 8192`, which equals 277 **only for k=1** because 277 and 8192 are coprime. **So no concatenation can ever be a legal fastfile** - the hypothesis was not merely untested, it was impossible. `lf_*`/`lf_hi_*` contain **zero** `IWff` occurrences.
> **The provenance finding**: the overlay's `mp_cross_fire.ff` (**41,648,405**) was a **2.6.9.7 (version word 365)** binary with **exactly one byte patched at `0x8`** (`0x6D -> 0xCD`) to claim version 461. The whole overlay was a 365 resource set masquerading as 461. The true 461 extraction is **37,331,221** bytes (4557 blocks, zone 75,189,466, **240 assets**).
> **What was fixed in the overlay**: `common_gametype_mp.ff` **34,783,232 (`mod 0x2000 = 0`, structurally illegal)** -> **34,693,397** (legal, 1400 assets); `mp_cross_fire.ff` -> the true-461 **37,331,221**. **All 23 ff files now satisfy `mod 0x2000 == 277`.**
> **The decisive run with that all-true-461 set**: **`engine_ready=True`**, samples **net 8 / 9 / 10**, entity count 1, **but `ui_state` stayed 5 and `[+0x5E8]` stayed 3** - identical to the old 365-repatch behaviour. **So the resource layer is NOT the blocker and can be considered settled.** (The earlier "swapping both files prevents startup" was a **launcher 30-second timeout misread**, not a crash.)
> **The cheapest decisive test now available**: **play a demo**. `mp_crash_tropical` - the map every 2021-08 demo was recorded on - is **already a complete, legal, true-461 set in the overlay**, and 22 demos are on disk. **If the world renders, the renderer and map pipeline are fine and everything missing is on the session/data side; if it still shows a spinner, this build cannot render that map at all, which is a hard limit worth knowing.**
> Acceptance: a screenshot showing the map AND `ui_state != 5`. > **2026-10-23 [THE DECISION THAT SETS STATE 3: an 8-byte comparison at `[obj+0x5FC]`, which reads like a session-token check]**
> The code at `0xBA3C05`:
> - `0xBA3C05`: **`push 8 ; lea edx,[ebp-0xC] ; lea eax,[esi+0x5FC]`**;
> - **`0xBA3C12`: `call 0xB73FE0` - compare the 8 bytes at `[obj+0x5FC]` with the 8 bytes at `[ebp-0xC]`**;
> - **`0xBA3C1A`: `jne 0xBA3C62`** - **if not equal, a different branch**;
> - `0xBA3C21`: `cmp [obj+0x644],0 ; jne` - skip the call if the flag is set;
> - `0xBA3C30`: `call 0x8435D0` with `[obj+0x640]`;
> - `0xBA3C3B`: **`[obj+0x5EC] = 1 ; [obj+0x5F0] = 1`**;
> - **`0xBA3C47`: `[obj+0x5E8] = 3`**.
> **What that means**: **state 3 is entered when an 8-byte value at `[obj+0x5FC]` equals an 8-byte value supplied by the caller** - **an 8-byte equality check on a connection object is most naturally a session id or handshake token**. **Our client IS at state 3, so that comparison already succeeded** - **which means state 3 is not the failure point: it is the state the client is in after a successful token comparison, and something must then move it onward.**
> **What this implies**: **the `0xBA3xxx` region is a session state machine** - **0 idle, 1/2 intermediate, 3 token-matched-and-waiting** - **and the transition out of 3 has not been located**. **Because state 3 is reached by a successful 8-byte comparison, the missing transition is most likely gated on a further message or on a timer rather than on the token.**
> Acceptance: a screenshot showing the map AND `ui_state != 5`. Evidence: [state3 token compare](evidence/experiments/20261023-codex-state3-token-compare.json), [state field writers](evidence/experiments/20261023-codex-state-field-writers.json).

> | address | value | note |

> | **`0xBA3DA3`** | **2** | |

> **What this gives**: **the states are 0, 1, 2 and 3**, written by handlers **clustered at `0xBA3xxx`** - **the same region as the status function `0xBA0780`**. **State 3 is set together with zeroing two adjacent counters**, which **reads like "entering a waiting phase"**, and **since our live value is 3, the client is sitting in exactly that phase**.

> **2026-10-23 [CORRECTION of round 252 + measured values: `[+0x5E8] == 3` is what PRODUCES status 2, so the client is waiting for that field to leave 3]**
> The three deciding fields, read live: **`[sub+0xC8] = 2`**, **`[sub+0x644] = 0`**, **`[sub+0x5E8] = 3`**, `ui_state` 5, `net_state` 10 (sub-object `0x42535E70`).
> **The code re-read**: **path B is taken because `[+0x644] == 0`**; `[+0xC8] == 2` so execution continues; **`xor eax,eax` -> 0**; **`cmp dword [ecx+0x5E8],3 ; sete al`** -> **`al = 1` when the field equals 3**; **`inc eax`** -> **2 when equal, 1 when not**. **So status = 2 when `[+0x5E8] == 3`, and status = 1 otherwise.**
> **The correction**: **round 252 said "`[0x5E8] == 3` would return 1" - that was wrong**: **`sete` sets `al` to 1 and the following `inc eax` makes it 2**. **So `[+0x5E8] == 3` PRODUCES status 2**, which is **exactly the status we measure** - **and the client would leave the ui-5 screen when `[+0x5E8]` becomes anything other than 3.**
> **What that means**: **the single field that decides the screen is `[sub+0x5E8]`**, and **its current value 3 keeps the client on the waiting screen**. **The other two fields are already in their expected states**: **`[+0xC8] = 2`** (matching the code's branch) and **`[+0x644] = 0`**. **So there is exactly one condition left, and it is a field inside the client's connection object.**
> **The natural next question**: **what writes `[sub+0x5E8]`, and what do the values 0..5 mean** - **the field is at a fixed offset in a 0x1618-byte singleton, so a static search for stores to `[reg+0x5E8]` with `reg` derived from the object would identify the writer**, **the same technique that found the singleton creator, and it does not need a running client.**
> Acceptance: a screenshot showing the map AND `ui_state != 5`. Evidence: [substate 3 produces wait](evidence/experiments/20261023-codex-substate-3-produces-wait.json), [connection state machine](evidence/experiments/20261023-codex-connection-state-machine.json).
> **2026-10-23 [THE CONNECTION STATE MACHINE: status is a mapping of `[netobj+0xC8]` plus two flags, and `[+0x5E8] == 3` is the most specific condition that would flip the screen]**
> `0xBA0780` read in full:
> - `0xBA0780`: `cmp [ecx+0x644],0`; `0xBA0787`: `eax = [ecx+0xC8]` - **the raw connection state**;
> - **path A** (`[0x644] != 0`): **if `[0xC8]` is 1 or 2 -> return 2**; otherwise return `[0xC8]`;
> - **path B** (`[0x644] == 0`): if `[0xC8] != 2` return it; **if `[0xC8] == 2` then `eax = ([0x5E8] == 3) + 1`**, i.e. **return 1 when `[0x5E8] == 3`, else 2**.
> **How status 2 is reached**: **path A** with `[0x644] != 0` and `[0xC8]` in {1,2}, **or path B** with `[0x644] == 0`, `[0xC8] == 2` and `[0x5E8] != 3`. **We measured status 2, so one of those holds.**
> **What would leave `ui_state` 5**: **the ui-5 branch at `0x8037D6` is taken when the mapped status equals 2**, so **the client leaves that screen when the status becomes anything else** - **either `[0xC8]` moves out of {1,2} / {2}, or `[0x5E8]` becomes 3 while `[0xC8]` stays 2**. **So `[0x5E8] == 3` is the most specific single condition that would flip the screen.**
> **What `0x5E8` likely is**: **a sub-state of the connection** - **in this protocol family the client distinguishes between being connected to the server and having the session handshake finished**, so **`[0x5E8] == 3` would mean the deeper handshake completed, which is exactly the layer `net_state` 10 does not cover.**
> **The next measurement if work continues**: **read `[netobj+0x644]`, `[netobj+0xC8]` and `[netobj+0x5E8]`** in the live client - **those three values pin down which path is taken and therefore which one has to move.**
> Acceptance: a screenshot showing the map AND `ui_state != 5`. Evidence: [connection state machine](evidence/experiments/20261023-codex-connection-state-machine.json), [object is the connection](evidence/experiments/20261023-codex-object-is-the-connection.json).
> **2026-10-23 [MAJOR REINTERPRETATION: the object holds `127.0.0.1` and status 2, and `[+0x4F8] = 1` forces that status - so `ui_state` 5 is very likely a CONNECTION screen, not a map-loading screen]**
> Read the live object and its sub-object:
> - **object `0x424EDBE8`**, **`[+0x4F4]` = `0x42425E70`** (a sub-object), **`[+0x4F8]` = `1`**;
> - **sub-object first 16 bytes**: `f4a4d500 02000000 7f000001 0df0adba`;
> - decoded: **`0x00D5A4F4` a vtable**, **`0x00000002` = STATUS 2**, **`0x0100007F` = .0.0.1**, **`0xBAADF00D`**.
> **The status logic at `0xB7A670`**: `ecx = [obj+0x4F4]` (null → status 0); `call 0xBA0780` gives a status; **`cmp byte [obj+0x4F8],0 ; jne` → return the status unchanged**; **only if `[+0x4F8] == 0` AND the status is 2 does it return 1**. **With `[+0x4F8] = 1` the status passes through as 2**, and **`0x8037D6` takes the ui-5 branch**.
> **Why this changes the picture**: **the sub-object contains the SERVER's IP address**, so **this object is about the NETWORK CONNECTION rather than about loading map assets**. **Status 2 with an address set reads like a connection state, not load progress.** **So `ui_state` 5 is most plausibly the CONNECTING screen** - **which also explains the spinner: a connecting UI animates it** - **and the client would then be stuck at "connected to 127.0.0.1 but the session is not established", not at "loading the map".**
> **What that points at**: **the network layer reads `net_state` 10, but the client's own connection object still reports status 2**. **That mismatch is the thing to explain**: **something in the session setup** (not the map, not the snapshots) **leaves the connection object in status 2**. **Candidates are the parts of the session handshake that follow gamestate**: **the client's acknowledgement path, or a session-level message our server does not send.**
> Acceptance: a screenshot showing the map AND `ui_state != 5`. Evidence: [object is the connection](evidence/experiments/20261023-codex-object-is-the-connection.json), [loader is a lazy singleton](evidence/experiments/20261023-codex-loader-is-a-lazy-singleton.json).
> **2026-10-23 [The loader object is a LAZY SINGLETON of `0x1618` bytes, and `ui_state` 5 is chosen when its status equals 2]**
> The getter at `0x803830`: **`eax = [0x8269774]`; if non-null return it**; otherwise **`push 0x1618 ; call 0xB74220` (allocate 5656 bytes)**, **`call 0xB82130` (construct)**, **`[0x8269774] = eax` (cache the singleton)**, then **`call 0xB7A400` with parameter `0xE39B6E8`**, a **4-byte allocation**, and **`call 0xB7A640` attaching it**.
> **What that tells us**: **the object is created on demand and cached**, so **its existence means "the subsystem is in use", not "a load is in progress"**. **And the earlier `0x4F8` estimate was wrong: the allocation is `0x1618` bytes** - **the destructor's `[esi+0x4F4]` access was just one field of a much larger object**.
> **Where `ui_state` 5 actually comes from**: **`0x803780` reads the object, calls `0xB838A0` and then `0xB7A670`, and compares the result with 2**; **when that result equals 2 it takes the branch at `0x8037FA`, which is where `ui_state` becomes 5**. **So `ui_state` 5 == "the loader object reports status 2"**, **and the spinner animating means the status stays 2 for as long as the client is stuck.**
> **The next question if work continues**: **what moves the object's status away from 2** - that is inside **`0xB838A0` and `0xB7A670`**, which take the object and return its state. **Since the object's initialisation left `0xBAADF00D` in two slots, a plausible reading is that the status cannot advance until those slots are filled, and the code that fills them is what never runs.**
> Acceptance: a screenshot showing the map AND `ui_state != 5`. Evidence: [loader is a lazy singleton](evidence/experiments/20261023-codex-loader-is-a-lazy-singleton.json), [spinner animates still loading](evidence/experiments/20261023-codex-spinner-animates-still-loading.json).
> **2026-10-23 [DECISIVE: two screenshots one second apart DIFFER - the spinner is animating, so the client is genuinely STILL LOADING]**
> Captured twice, one second apart, at net 10 with one entity and `ui_state` 5:
> **`codex-r237-a.png` = 10752 bytes**, **`codex-r237-b.png` = 10690 bytes**, **identical = False**.
> **What it settles**: **the spinner is animating**, therefore **the client is drawing a loading animation rather than a frozen undrawn world**. **So the "in the map but nothing rendered" hypothesis that the teardown-path finding had reopened is FALSE.** **The client is genuinely stuck inside its load sequence** - **exactly as the user's own description says: map loading, waiting for other players, loading player data, black load.**
> **Why this needed testing**: **the only code that clears the loader object is a teardown path**, which suggested **the object could legitimately be alive while in a map**. **If that had been true, the black frame would have been a rendering failure with the load already complete.** **The animating spinner rules that out**: **a completed load would not keep animating a spinner.**
> **The conclusion chain that now stands**: **the network handshake completes** (net 10); **the snapshot header parses**; **all five content blocks are entered**; **the entity count becomes 1, an id is stored, and a mode-1 delta writes real floats into the entity struct**; **and the client STILL animates a loading spinner**, **so its load sequence has not finished**. **Therefore the missing condition is inside the client's load sequence and is not carried by any of the snapshot-side levers that were tried.**
> Acceptance: a screenshot showing the map AND `ui_state != 5`. Evidence: [spinner animates still loading](evidence/experiments/20261023-codex-spinner-animates-still-loading.json), [loader is torn down not completed](evidence/experiments/20261023-codex-loader-is-torn-down-not-completed.json).
> **2026-10-23 [REINTERPRETATION: the loading object is destroyed on UNLOAD/shutdown, not when loading completes]**
> The only code that clears `[0x8269774]` is a **teardown path** at `0x77D043`:
> - `0x77D043`: `cmp [0x8269774],ebx ; je 0x77D092` - skip if already null;
> - `0x77D050`: `[0x84ABB04] = 1` - a flag set before teardown;
> - `0x77D05A`: `call [0xCA819C]` - **acquire a guard**;
> - `0x77D06A`: `call 0xB82100` - **a method on the object**;
> - `0x77D079`: `edx=[ecx] ; eax=[edx] ; push 1 ; call eax` - **the DELETING DESTRUCTOR**;
> - `0x77D086`: **`mov [0x8269774],0`** - clear the global;
> - `0x77D08C`: `call [0xCA8190]` - **release the guard**;
> - `0x77D092`: `call 0x808940 ; call 0x66B360` - **further shutdown work**.
> **What this changes**: **I had been treating "the object is non-null" as "the frontend is still loading"**. **But the only code that clears it is a teardown path** - **so while a map is active the object is EXPECTED to be non-null, and its presence is not evidence of loading**. **Which means `ui_state = 5` is also not proven to mean "still loading"** - **it may simply be the UI state used for both the loading screen and an in-game frame that has nothing to draw.**
> **What that reopens**: **the "world not drawn" hypothesis returns** - **the client may be in the map with a valid UI state**, **and the black frame with a spinner may be the absence of scene content rather than an unfinished load**. **And the spinner could be a UI element drawn whenever the renderer has no valid view, rather than a load indicator.**
> **How to distinguish the two**: **if the client is in the map, two screenshots a second apart should show the SAME frame; if it is still loading, the spinner should have moved.** **Two captures compared pixel-wise is a cheap and decisive test.**
> Acceptance: a screenshot showing the map AND `ui_state != 5`. Evidence: [loader is torn down not completed](evidence/experiments/20261023-codex-loader-is-torn-down-not-completed.json), [loading never completes](evidence/experiments/20261023-codex-loading-never-completes.json).
> **2026-10-23 [Advancing `serverTime` does NOT dismiss the loader - the last cheap snapshot-side lever is closed]**
> Built **eight copies** of the accepted body with **`serverTime` stepping 72200, 72450, ... 73950** and rotated them at 2 s: **`ui_state` stayed 5 and the loader object `0x4057DBE8` was held at every sample** (net 8 / 9 / 10). Screenshot `runs/codex-r236-shot.png`.
> **Conclusion**: **the world clock advancing does not satisfy the loader** - **the frontend's load task is not waiting for server time to progress**. **Together with the earlier negatives this closes the set of snapshot-side levers a server can pull.**
> **The full list of negatives**:
> - **core snapshot contents** (playerState fields, entity count, id, delta, position): **accepted, loader never clears**;
> - **`flags` `0x0C` -> `0x08`** (the exact baseline value cols writes): **no change**;
> - **an entity-free snapshot followed by entity snapshots**: **net 10 and count 1 coexist, `ui_state` stays 5**;
> - **all five content blocks covered**: **already the case**;
> - **advancing `serverTime` across eight snapshots**: **no change**.
> **What remains**: **the loader object is partially initialised** (`0xBAADF00D` in two slots) **and is a C++ instance of at least `0x4F8` bytes with vtable `0xD599DC`**. **Identifying what fills those slots needs symbolic information for this build or a memory-write breakpoint**, **neither of which the current harness offers** (fixed-address `int3` only). **So the remaining work is a tooling problem as much as an investigative one.**
> **Deliverables re-verified this round**: **`selfcheck: 8/8 passed`**; **evidence audit: 1295 records, invalid JSON 0**.

> The cols writer (`snapshot/mod.rs:899-915`) gives the header exactly:
> - **byte 0**: `svc_snapshot` (**0**);
> - **bytes 1..4**: `serverTime` little-endian;
> - **byte 5**: `delta_distance` (**0 when establishing a baseline**);
> - **byte 6: FLAGS - `8` when establishing a baseline, `0` otherwise**;
> - then **bits**: `1` bit no-prior-playerState, `1` bit transmit-origin, **`8` bits `last_changed + 1`**, `1` bit field gap, `1` bit `-97` codec, then **4 bytes commandTime**, then the fields.
> **What our body actually has** (`single22`, hybrid and mode1 identically): **`00 08 1a 01 00 00 0c 96 07 60 00 18`** -> **svc 0, serverTime 72200, delta_distance 0, flags = 12 = `0b1100` = `8 | 4`**.
> **Verdict**: **the BASELINE bit (8) IS set** - so we do declare a baseline - **but an EXTRA bit (4) is also set that cols never sets in either mode**.
> **Why this is a real finding**: **a wrong flag is exactly the kind of thing that would make the client accept the snapshot's contents** (**which it does: count 1, id decoded**) **yet never finish loading**. **And it is a ONE-BYTE change to test: 12 -> 8.**

> **2026-10-23 [`ui_state` is driven by a LOADING OBJECT at `[0x8269774]` - while it is non-null the loading screen is shown, when it clears `ui_state` drops to 0]**
> The update function at `0x803780`:
> - **`0x803781`: `esi = [0x8269774]`** - **the loading object**;
> - **`0x803787`: `test esi,esi ; jne 0x8037AB`** - **if the object exists, run its update path**;
> - `0x80378B`: `eax = [0x84ABA50]` (ui_state); **if 0, return unchanged**;
> - `0x803794`: `[0x84ABA54] = eax` - **save the previous ui_state**;
> - **`0x803799`: `[0x84ABA50] = 0`** - **clear ui_state**;
> - `0x80379F`: `[0xE4EA3C] = 0xDE16E0` - **a callback is installed**;
> - `0x8037AB`: **calls `0xB838A0` and `0xB7A670` on the object**; then **`0x8037D6`: `cmp esi,2 ; je 0x8037FA`** - **the object's status selects the branch**; **`0x8037E4`**: the non-2 branch **also clears ui_state**.

> **2026-10-23 [COMPARISON: the mode-1 body kept the client alive, the id-8 body killed it - so editing the id bytes damages the blocks that follow]**
> Two runs with **one entity and count = 1** in both:
> - **`snapshot-mode1.bin`**: edits **only bits 1330..1355** (inside the delta region) -> **state 9, process ALIVE and readable**, entity floats **3.58 / 1.0 / 0.1**;
> - **`snapshot-id8b.bin`**: edits **byte 165 = 0x01 and byte 166 &= 0xFE** -> **state 9, process GONE at the end**.
> **Why this is informative**: **both bodies carry one entity, so the entity itself is not the difference**. **`mode1` changed only bits inside the delta region and the client survived**; **`id8b` changed bytes 165 and 166, which lie AFTER the id in the body and therefore belong to whatever block follows the entity list**. **So the exit is caused by damaging the following blocks, not by the entity or its id.**
> **What that implies for id control**: **the id bits are not confined to bytes 163/165/166 in a way that is free of side effects** - **byte 165 and byte 166 are also data for later blocks**. **So an id can only be CHANGED at the cost of rewriting those later blocks consistently**, which means **the "small id" experiment cannot be done by a blind byte edit - the tail has to be rebuilt for the new id**.
> **The practical conclusion**: **the earlier 4048 id came from the untouched body and the client tolerated it in some runs (`mode1`) and not in others**, so **the id value itself is not what decides survival**. **What decides survival is whether the bytes after the entity list are still a valid continuation of the stream** - **the same lesson as the ps block: the snapshot is one stream and every edit propagates.**
> **Next**: **build the entity with the tail regenerated from the edit point instead of patching bytes in place**, so **the following blocks start from a consistent position** - **concretely: after the id, rewrite the remaining bits with the same generator that produced the working tail.**
> Acceptance: a screenshot showing the map. Evidence: [id edit damages tail](evidence/experiments/20261023-codex-id-edit-damages-tail.json), [id control verified](evidence/experiments/20261023-codex-id-control-verified.json).

> **2026-10-23 [EXACT AND VERIFIED: the 12-bit entity id is `(byte163 bits 5-7) | (byte165 << 3) | (byte166 bit 0 << 11)` - the reader SKIPS byte 164]**
> Verified against the body and the measurement:
> - **byte163 = 0x18, byte164 = 0x01 (the count), byte165 = 0xFA, byte166 = 0x1F**;
> - **assembly**: `low3 = (0x18 >> 5) & 7 = 0`; **`byte165 = 0xFA`**; **`bit0 of byte166 = 1`**;
> - **value = `0 | (0xFA << 3) | (1 << 11)` = `0x0FD0` = 4048** - **matches the measurement exactly**.

> **Why this took so long to find**: **the format mixes a byte-addressed field (the count) into the middle of a bit-addressed stream**, and **the reader's resumption rule uses the byte cursor rather than the bit position**, **so the two cursors diverge by exactly the byte that was consumed**. **Every attempt to treat the id as a contiguous 12-bit slice at 1309 was therefore off by one byte.**
> **The concrete recipe**: **count = byte 164** (`0x01` gives one entity); **id: write byte 163 bits 5-7 for the low 3 bits, byte 165 for bits 3..10, and bit 0 of byte 166 for bit 11**. **Example: id = 8 -> byte163 bits 5-7 = 0, byte165 = 0x01, byte166 bit 0 = 0.**

> The trace from the disassembly: **`0x67168F` calls `0x66ED70`** (the byte-based count reader, **which advances `[+0x1C]` only, not `[+0x20]`**); **`0x671698` stores the count byte**; **`0x6716A1` pushes `0xC`**; **`0x6716A3` sets `eax = esi`** (the stream); **`0x6716A5` calls `0x66EC30`** to read **12 bits from `[+0x20]`**; **`0x6716AA` loads `bl`** (the loop index); **`0x6716AD` stores `ax` to `word [ecx*2 + 0x7859358]`**.

> **2026-10-23 [0x66EC30 is a standard LSB-first bit reader - so id 4048 cannot come from bits 1309..1320, which means the probe's stream pointer is not the one used]**
> Read the assembly loop:
> - `0x66EC8D`: `cmp ecx,[esi+0x10] ; jge` -> zero if the byte index is past the bound;
> - **`0x66EC96`: the buffer is `[esi+8]`, the index is `[+0x20] >> 3`**;
> - **`0x66ECA3`: `shr eax, cl` with `cl = [+0x20] & 7`** - **align so the requested bit becomes bit 0**;
> - `0x66ECA5`: `ecx = 8 - offset` - bits available in this byte;
> - `0x66ECB1`: **if `N <= available`: `[+0x20] += N` and return `byte & mask`**;
> - `0x66ECCB`: **else consume the available bits and continue in the next byte**.
> **Conclusion about the encoding**: **the reader is a plain LSB-first bit reader over the byte buffer at `[esi+8]`**. **So a 12-bit read starting at bit 1309 returns exactly the 12 bits at 1309..1320** - **which are `000100000000` = 8** - **yet the client stored 4048**.
> **What that leaves**: **the read that produced 4048 did not start at bit 1309 of the same stream**. **The most likely reason is that the probe's `esi` at `0x6716C3` is not the stream used by `0x671650` for the id read** - the probe samples whatever `esi` holds at the loop-exit instruction, **which may already be a different register role**. **So the earlier "20 bits for a 12-bit read" measurement is suspect for the same reason**: **the two samples may come from different stream objects**.
> **The clean way to settle the id question**: **probe inside `0x671650` itself** (for example at **`0x66ECA1`, right after the byte fetch**) **and log `[esi+8]`, `[+0x20]` and the returned value** - **that ties the value to the exact position and buffer, with the same `esi` the decoder uses**.

> - **`snapshot-single22.bin`: count = 0, no entity -> state 10** (the in-match state this project has always reached);
> - **`ent2` / `ent4` / `mode1` / `mode5`: count = 1, one entity -> state 9 in every case**.
> **So the presence of an entity is what keeps the client on the loading screen**, and **it does not depend on what that entity's delta contains**, because **even a no-op delta gives the same result**.
> **The most likely cause**: **the entity id is 4048, which is out of range for a map like `mp_cross_fire`** (typical CoD entity counts are **in the hundreds to low thousands**). **A client that cannot resolve an entity in its list will not finish loading**, which is **exactly the observed behaviour** - **and the id is fully under our control: it is read as 12 bits from bit 1309**.
> **The decisive next experiment**: **rebuild the body with a SMALL entity id** (for example **1, 64 or 100**) **instead of the arbitrary 4048**, keeping everything else identical. **If the client then reaches state 10 with count = 1, the id range was the blocker and the entity pipeline is complete**; **if it stays at 9, the client needs something else besides a valid id**.
> **Why this is progress**: **it moves the failure from "the world is not drawn" to "the entity id is probably out of range", which is a one-line change**. **It also explains why every entity experiment so far ended on the loading screen: the id was never chosen, it fell out of the bit pattern at 1309.**

> **2026-10-23 [KEY: one mode operation per entity per snapshot - and mode 1 reads its position components INLINE, so a single mode-1 delta positions an entity]**
> **The exit `0x671A0D`**: it walks a list from `[0x77D8218]` comparing `[edi+0x18]` (the entity id), then **sets a bit in a bitset at `[0x77D821C]` using `id>>3` and `1<<(id&7)`** - **a "mark this entity as changed" step, then it returns**. **So `0x671700` processes ONE mode operation and returns** - it does **not** loop over further operations.
> **The consequence**: **modes 3 and 4 only set the stream scratch fields `[+0x24]`/`[+0x28]`**; **mode 1 and 8 read them**. **Since each snapshot carries one operation, a mode-3-then-mode-1 sequence would span two snapshots** - **but that is only needed for `[edi+0x10]` and `[edi+8]`**.
> **Why mode 1 ALONE is enough for a position**: **the three position components are read INLINE** by `0x6715D0`, `0x6714D0` and `0x671550` **from the bit stream, not from scratch**. **`0x6715D0` reads gate, scale and a 5-bit value and produces a float**, so **mode 1 by itself supplies everything needed to write `[edi+0x24]`, `[edi+0x2C]` and `[edi+0x28]`**. **The scratch-based fields would be zero, but the entity would still have a real position.**
> **The body to build**: **changed bit = 0**; **mode selector must produce mode 1** (the first bit at 1330 = 1 for the `value+1` branch, with the two value bits = 0, giving mode = 1); **mode 1 payload = 2 bits inline, then three component blocks of `gate(1) + scale(1) + value(5)`**. **Suggested values**: component 1 = **gate 1, scale 1, value 20 (+100 units)**; components 2 and 3 = **gate 1, scale 0, value 0**.
> **Next**: **emit exactly that body** and **probe the entity struct floats at `+0x24`, `+0x28`, `+0x2C` for entity 4048** - **the first time a deliberately chosen position should appear in the client's entity state**.

> **2026-10-23 [THE SCALE CONSTANT IS 5.0 - a position component is a delta of `value × 1.0` or `value × 5.0` with a 5-bit value]**
> Read the component encoding inside mode 1:
> - **gate (1 bit)** - `0` means the component is **unchanged**;
> - **scale (1 bit)** - `1` selects **the constant at `0xDB1118`**, `0` selects **1.0**;
> - **value (5 bits)** via `0x66EC30`;
> - **`0xDB1118` = 5.0** (read directly from the image as a float32);
> - **arithmetic**: `component = value * (scale ? 5.0 : 1.0)`, applied as a **delta** to the entity's previous position.
> **What that gives us**: **resolution 1 unit (scale 0) or 5 units (scale 1)**; **range per update 0..31 or 0..155 units**; **cost 7 bits per component, about 21 bits for a full origin**.
> **Why this completes the recipe**: **the entity's position is delta-coded**, and **its initial value is whatever the entity struct already holds**, so **the first update can place the entity anywhere within 155 units of that initial value**. **Combined with the earlier findings, a positioned entity needs**: **mode 3 selector + 11-bit value**, **mode 4 selector + `-97` value**, **mode 1 selector + 2-bit value**, **then three component blocks of gate + scale + 5-bit value**. **Every one of those is a plain bit sequence the existing `BitWriter` can emit.**
> **The one remaining unknown**: **the exact FPU arithmetic after the 5-bit read** (`0x67160F`) - **whether it adds the scaled value to a stored float or replaces it**. **That decides absolute vs relative positioning** but **does not block the experiment**: **any non-zero component will produce a visible change if the entity is drawn**.
> **Next**: **emit the three-operation delta with a non-trivial origin** (for example **scale 1, value 20** on the first component) **and observe whether the entity's float fields at `+0x24/+0x28/+0x2C` become non-zero** - **the last step before the client has a positioned entity**.

> **2026-10-23 [DECISIVE: mode 1 writes THREE FLOATS into the entity at `+0x24`, `+0x28` and `+0x2C` - that is the entity's ORIGIN]**
> The commit tail at `0x671873`:
> - **`0x671873`: `call 0x6715D0 ; fstp dword [edi+0x24]`** - a **float**, first position component;
> - **`0x67187B`: `call 0x6714D0 ; fstp dword [edi+0x2C]`** - second component;
> - **`0x671883`: `call 0x671550 ; fstp dword [edi+0x28]`** - third component;
> - `0x67188B`: `jmp 0x671A0D` - **the common exit of the delta decoder**.
> **The complete list of what mode 1 writes**: `[edi+0x10]` = the value accumulated by **mode 3** (11-bit); `[edi+8]` = the value accumulated by **mode 4** (`-97`); `[edi+0x30]` = a **2-bit value read inline**; `[edi+0x18]` = an **id looked up from the entity id array** (mode 1 only); **`[edi+0x24]`, `[edi+0x2C]`, `[edi+0x28]` = three FLOATS, i.e. the entity ORIGIN**.
> **Why this is the answer to the original question**: **the goal has been to give an entity an `eType` and an `origin` so the client draws it**. **Mode 1 is precisely the operation that writes the origin as three floats**, and **the three floats are computed by `0x6715D0`, `0x6714D0` and `0x671550` from the accumulated scratch values** - so **the position is derived from the mode 3 / mode 4 accumulators**. **That means a three-operation delta (mode 3, mode 4, mode 1) is exactly what places an entity at a chosen position.**
> **The immediate next step**: **read `0x6715D0`, `0x6714D0` and `0x671550`** to learn **how each float is derived from the scratch values**, **then choose mode 3 and mode 4 values that produce the desired x, y, z**. **Mode 1 also needs its 2-bit inline value and, when the id width is non-zero, an id index** - **those are cheap to supply**.

> **2026-10-23 [STRUCTURE FOUND: the entity modes are a PIPELINE - modes 3/4 accumulate, modes 1/8 commit into the entity struct]**
> Classified all 13 handlers by whether they read bits and where they write:
> - **modes that read bits**: **1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 11, 12, 13**;
> - **modes that only copy**: **5, 6, 7, 9, 10**.
> **Modes 3 and 4 are ACCUMULATORS**: **mode 3 (`0x6717A1`) reads 11 bits into `[esi+0x24]`**; **mode 4 (`0x6717B5`) reads one `-97` value into `[esi+0x28]`**.
> **Mode 1 (`0x671890`) is a COMMIT**:
> - `0x671890`: `eax = [esi+0x24]`; **`0x671893`: `[edi+0x10] = eax`**;
> - `0x671896`: `ecx = [esi+0x28]`; **`0x67189D`: `[edi+8] = ecx`**;
> - `0x6718A0`: **read 2 bits**; **`0x6718A5`: `[edi+0x30] = eax`**;
> - `0x6718A8`: `cl = [0x7859559]` (**the entity-id width computed by the list parser**); **if set, read `cl` bits**; **`0x6718C5`: `eax = word [eax*2 + 0x7859358]`** (index into the id array); **`0x6718CD`: `[edi+0x18] = eax`**.
> **Mode 8 (`0x6718D2`) is a partial commit**: same `[edi+0x10]`, `[edi+8]`, `[edi+0x30]` writes **without** the `[edi+0x18]` cross-entity reference.
> **Why this is a structural insight**: **the delta is NOT a field loop and NOT a single field - it is a SEQUENCE of mode-coded operations**. **Modes 3 and 4 write into stream scratch fields (`+0x24`, `+0x28`)**; **modes 1 and 8 take those scratch values and write them into the entity struct at `+0x10`, `+8`, `+0x30` and (mode 1 only) `+0x18`**. **So a real entity update looks like: `[mode 3: set scratch A][mode 4: set scratch B][mode 1: commit A and B into the entity]`** - **and that explains why single-mode bodies changed nothing visible: the scratch values were never committed**.
> **The concrete target now**: **emit a three-operation delta - mode 3 (11-bit value), mode 4 (`-97` value), mode 1 (commit)** - **then the entity struct at `[edi+0x10]`, `[+8]` and `[+0x30]` receives real values**. **`+0x10` and `+8` are the first two fields of the 0x58-byte entity state, which is where a position would live.**

> Read the payload loop and the decoder behind it:
> - **`0x471DE3`**: index from the frame clock, **`edi = &entityRing[i]` with stride `0x34` (52 bytes)**;
> - **`0x471E03`: `call 0x447190` -> READ 1 BIT (the per-entity changed flag)**;
> - **`0x471E0E`: if the bit is 1** -> **read N bits** (`N = [ebp+8]`, the id width) and **copy 13 dwords (52 bytes) into the entity ring slot**;
> - **`0x471E4A`: if the bit is 0** -> **`call 0x671700` - the per-entity DELTA decoder**;
> - `0x471E59`: `test eax,eax ; jne 0x471DDA` - **loop for the next entity**.
> **The delta decoder `0x671700` starts with a MODE SELECTOR**: `[ebp-4] = 3` initially; `0x671722` reads **1 bit** and, when set, **2 more bits -> mode = value + 1**; `0x67173F` reads a bit and, when set, **2 bits -> mode = value + 5**; a third branch reads yet another bit. **So the payload begins with a variable-length selector that chooses a delta MODE.**
> **What our body actually has**: **bits 1329..1350 = `1111000001111111111110`**, so **bit 1329 = 1** - **the changed flag is set**, and **the client reads N bits and copies a struct instead of decoding a delta**. **That is not what a fresh entity should do, and is a plausible cause of the exit.**
> **Next**: **clear bit 1329 to 0** so the changed flag is 0 and **the delta decoder runs**, then **observe whether the client survives the snapshot and what mode the selector picks**.

> **What this fixes for the payload**: **the per-entity payload begins at bit 1329 for this body** (one entity, id 4048), **so the first payload field is read from 1329** - **any payload we write must be placed at 1329, not at 1309 + 12**.

> **What 1307 means**: the bit reader keeps `[+0x20]` as an **absolute bit position**, so **the entity block begins at bit 1307**. **Gate bit 1 = bit 1307**, **gate bit 2 = bit 1308**. **Bit 1307 is the LAST bit of the 1308-bit hybrid header** (bits 1300..1307 are all ones there), and **bit 1308 is the first bit of our playerState block, which we set to 1 (`has-ps`)**. **So BOTH gate bits should read 1.**
> **The puzzle**: if both gates read 1, the code falls through to the count reader `0x66ED70`, **which reads the byte at the BYTE cursor `[+0x1C] = 164`, i.e. `body[164]`** - and **in `snapshot-ent1.bin` `body[164]` was set to `0x01`, yet the count STILL read 0**. **So either the gates did not both read 1, or `0x66ED70` reads from a different base than the body start.**
> **The two consistent explanations**: **(a)** the gate is **not the first read** of the block - `0x471DA3` calls `0x671650` and something before that **consumes bits**, so the effective gate indices are **higher than 1307/1308**; **(b)** `0x66ED70` reads at `[stream+0x1C]` but **that field is an index into a buffer whose base is `[stream+8]` or `[stream+0xC]`, not the body start** - **the disassembly shows two different buffers selected by comparing against `[stream+0x14]`**.
> **Next**: read the two buffers in `0x66ED70` - **`[edx+8]` and `[edx+0xC]` are two separate pointers**, and **the read picks one depending on whether the cursor is below or above the window start**; **probing both pointers at `0x671650` tells us which buffer `body[164]` actually lives in**.
> Acceptance: a screenshot showing the map. Evidence: [entity block at bit 1307](evidence/experiments/20261023-codex-entity-block-at-bit-1307.json), [one position two units](evidence/experiments/20261023-codex-one-position-two-units.json).
> **2026-10-23 [CORRECTION: `[+0x1C]` and `[+0x20]` are ONE position in two units, not two cursors]**
> Read the bit reader **`0x447190`**:
> - `0x447194`: `cmp [edx],0 ; je 0x4471A0` - return -1 if the stream is already in error;
> - **`0x4471A0`: `ecx = [edx+0x20] & 7`** - the **bit offset inside the current byte**;
> - `0x4471AC`: `esi = [edx+0x18] + [edx+0x14]` - the bound;
> - **`0x4471B2`: `eax = [edx+0x1C]`** - the **byte index**; overrun sets `[edx]=1` and returns -1;
> - **`0x4471C7`: `esi = eax*8 ; [edx+0x20] = esi ; [edx+0x1C] = eax+1`** - **when starting a new byte the byte index advances and the bit position is set to `byte*8`**;
> - **`0x4471D6`: `ebx = [edx+0x20]`** = the **absolute bit position**; `0x4471DF`: `eax = ebx >> 3` = the **byte index derived from it**.
> **The correction**: the earlier note said the snapshot has **"two independent cursors, one in bits and one in bytes"** - **that is WRONG**. **`[+0x20]` is the absolute bit position and `[+0x1C]` is the byte index of the SAME stream**, and **the bit reader keeps them consistent**; **the byte reader `0x66ED70` also advances `[+0x1C]`**, so **a byte read moves the same position forward by a byte**. **There is ONE logical position, exposed in two units** - **and mixing the units is what made the earlier interpretation look strange**.
> **What this gives us**: **`[+0x20]` at `0x671650` entry is EXACTLY the bit index of the first gate bit**; **the second is `[+0x20]+1`**, and **the count byte is read at the byte containing the position after those two bits**. **So one more probe reading `[+0x20]` pins both gate bits precisely - the last unknown before the gates can be set deliberately.**
> **Next**: extend the `Cursor` probe to **also log `[+0x20]`** and re-run with `single22`; then **set the two gate bits at exactly those indices** and check whether **the count reader is reached**.

> Patched `single22` at **byte 164 = `0x01`** (`runs/snapshot-ent1.bin`) and re-ran. **The byte cursor is still 164 and the length still 172**, so the patched byte **was in the right place for a BYTE read** - **but the count is still 0**, the entity ids are all zero, and **the state moved from 10 to 9**.

> **2026-10-23 [CURSORS MEASURED: the entity count is read from **byte 164** of a 172-byte body, while the bit cursor is far ahead]**
> The probe at **`0x671650`** (a plain function entry, the shape that has worked before) fired: **stream `0x16D9EC`**, **`[+0x14] = 172`**, **`[+0x18] = 0`**, **`[+0x1C] = 164`**, **`[+0x24] = 0xFFFFFFFF`**, state 10.

| field | value | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `+0x14` | **172** | the **total length of our body** (`snapshot-single22.bin` is exactly 172 bytes) |
| `+0x18` | 0 | window start |
| `+0x1C` | **164** | **the BYTE CURSOR when the entity block starts** |
| `+0x24` | `0xFFFFFFFF` | the sentinel the caller writes before each block |

> **The actionable conclusion**: **the entity COUNT is read from byte offset 164 of the body**. The formula in `0x66ED70` is **bound = `[+0x18] + [+0x14]` = 172**, **cursor = `[+0x1C]` = 164**, so **the byte read is `body[164]`**. **The bit cursor is around bit 1350 at that moment** - **a completely different position** - so **the two cursors are indeed independent, and the count is NOT where a pure bit model would put it**. **Therefore: to make the entity count equal 1, `body[164]` must be `0x01`.**

> **2026-10-23 [THE SNAPSHOT HAS TWO CURSORS: the bit reader and a separate BYTE reader - and the entity COUNT comes from the byte one]**
> Read **`0x66ED70`** (the entity-count reader called at `0x67168F`):
> - **`0x66ED70`**: `eax = [edx+0x18]; ecx = [edx+0x1C]; esi = [edx+0x14]`;
> - `0x66ED7C`: `cmp ecx,eax ; jge 0x66EDB5` - **overrun: set the error flag and return -1**;
> - **`0x66ED8D`: `movzx eax, byte [eax+ecx]` - RETURN ONE BYTE**;
> - **`0x66ED91`: `inc ecx ; [edx+0x1C] = ecx` - advance the BYTE cursor**.
> **What this proves**: **`0x66ED70` is NOT a bit reader** - it returns a **whole byte** and advances a **byte cursor at `[+0x1C]`**, while **the bit reader used everywhere else (`0x447190` / `0x66EC30`) advances a different cursor**. **So the snapshot stream carries TWO cursors: one in bits, one in bytes** - and **the entity COUNT is taken from the BYTE stream**, while **the two gate bits before it come from the BIT stream**.
> **Why this dissolves a lot of confusion**: the project has been treating the snapshot as **one continuous bit stream**. **If the count is byte-addressed, then inserting or removing bits anywhere before it changes which BYTE it reads** - **which explains why tiny changes at the ps block shifted the entity interpretation in ways that looked erratic**, and **means the body must be built with BOTH a bit layout and a byte layout in mind**.
> **The recipe, revised**: **bit 1 = 1** and **bit 2 = 1** (bit stream); **then the next BYTE read by the byte cursor must be `0x01`** (count = 1); **then 12 bits give the entity id**. **So the payload has to be arranged so that the byte cursor lands on a `0x01` byte at that moment.**
> **Next**: find **where the byte cursor `[+0x1C]` is initialised** for a snapshot - **whether it starts at the same offset as the bit cursor or at a byte-aligned position** - since `0x66ED70` reads `[edx+0x1C]` directly, **a probe on the stream struct just before the entity block reveals both cursors at once**.
> Acceptance: a screenshot showing the map. Evidence: [two cursors](evidence/experiments/20261023-codex-two-cursors.json), [entity list layout](evidence/experiments/20261023-codex-entity-list-layout.json).
> **2026-10-23 [THE ENTITY LIST LAYOUT, READ FROM `0x671650`: two gate bits, a count, then 12 bits per entity id]**
> The entity block starts at `0x471DA3` with **`call 0x671650`**; **if it returns 0 the whole block is skipped** (`je 0x471E88`). **`0x671650` is the entity-list decoder**:
> - **`0x671650`**: `memset(0x7859358, 0, 0x1204)` - **clear the entity id list**;
> - **`0x671661`**: `memset(0x785955A, 0xFF, 0x1001)` - clear the second array;
> - **`0x671678`**: **READ BIT 1**; if 0 -> `0x6716F0`;
> - **`0x671685`**: **READ BIT 2**; if 0 -> `0x6716ED`;
> - **`0x67168F`**: `call 0x66ED70` -> read a value; **`0x671698`: `mov [0x7859558], al`** - **THIS IS THE ENTITY COUNT, stored as a BYTE**;
> - **`0x6716A1`**: `call 0x66EC30` with `push 0xC` -> **READ 12 BITS per entity id**; `0x6716AD` stores it; `0x6716BF` loops **count** times.
> **Why the count read as `0xFFFF0000`**: the count is a **BYTE at `0x7859558`**, so the dword was **`0x00` plus two `0xFF` neighbours** - **exactly what the `0xFF` memset at `0x671661` leaves**. **So the count really is ZERO**, and **the block either took one of the two gate branches, or `0x66ED70` returned 0**.
> **The recipe to get ONE entity**: **bit 1 = 1**, **bit 2 = 1**, **then the count must decode to 1**, **then 12 bits give the entity id**.
> **Next**: read **`0x66ED70`** to learn how the count is encoded - **the only unknown left in this recipe** - then build a body with **bit1 = 1, bit2 = 1, count = 1** and check that **`0x7859558` reads 1**.

> Re-ran with the **exact** record match. Results: **`GateConst` (`0x47226D`): 1 hit, `edi = 0x0`**; **`GateTest` (`0x47239A`): 0 hits**.

> **2026-10-23 [CONSOLIDATION: field writes already work for two different landing indices with clean parses - the codec is NOT the remaining blocker]**

|---|---|---|---|---|

The remaining `value 5`/`value 6` anomalies (**extra 21-bit units**) are about **what the decoder reads AFTER the field**, not about **whether the field itself can be written** - and those 21-bit steps are consistent with **the block simply continuing into further iterations**, which is **expected** when the trailing bits look like a header.

> **2026-10-23 [THREE DISTINCT LENGTHS in arithmetic progression: 55, 76, 97 - a step of exactly 21 bits]**
> Tested **value 5 (`0b101`)**: **ps = 76 bits**, **`error 0`** - a THIRD length, between the two known ones.

| value | binary | ps bits | ps error |
|---|---|---|---|
| 255 | 0b11111111 | 55 | 0 |
| 256 / 512 / 1024 / 2048 / 4096 | single bit | 55 | 0 |
| **5** | **0b101** | **76** | **0** |
| **6** | **0b110** | **97** | **1** |
| 5830 | many bits | 97 | 1 |

> **The arithmetic**: `55 = 22 non-value bits + 33 value bits` (the `gate = 1` form of codec `-97`); then **`76 = 55 + 21`** and **`97 = 76 + 21`** - **each extra unit costs exactly 21 bits**.
> **What a 21-bit unit could be**: a **further delta record** (`continuation 1 + V 5 + distance + a small value` lands near 21), so **the value's remaining bits are most likely being read as a NEW field header**, producing **one or two extra decoded fields**. That also explains **why value 6 raises a stream error** - after two extra units the decoder runs past the terminator.
> **Why the high values are clean**: **255, 256, 512, 1024, 2048 and 4096 all cost exactly 55**, so for those the decoder consumed the 33-bit field **and stopped**. The difference must be in **how the low bits of the value look to the decoder AFTER the field** - a value whose trailing bits happen to look like a valid header **continues**, others do not.
> **Next**: read **what `0x66EC30` does with the 8-bit form** (`push 8`) - the N-bit reader used by both branches, whose exact bit order matters - **then construct a body whose value bits keep the parse at 55**.
> Acceptance: a screenshot showing the map. Evidence: [step 21](evidence/experiments/20261023-codex-step-21.json), [codec -97 read](evidence/experiments/20261023-codex-codec-minus97-read.json).
> **2026-10-23 [READ THE CODEC: `-97` is a 1-bit gate followed by EITHER 32 bits OR 8 bits (a signed offset from a baseline)]**
> Followed the dispatch in `0x6701D0`: **`0x67069C: cmp ecx,-0x61`** (`-97`) -> **`0x670BBF`**, which does `mov eax,[ebp+0xC]; mov ecx,esi; call 0x66F9E0; [ebx]=eax`. The reader **`0x66F9E0`**:
> - `0x66F9EA`: **`edi = arg3` - a BASELINE value**;
> - `0x66F9EC`: **read 1 bit (the gate)**;
> - **gate = 1** -> `0x66FA0B`: **read the full 32 bits** and return them;
> - **gate = 0** -> `0x66F9F5`: **`push 8; call 0x66EC30` = read 8 bits**, then **`value = baseline - that`**.
> **The cost**: **gate 1 -> 1 + 32 = 33 bits**; **gate 0 -> 1 + 8 = 9 bits**. **Both forms are FIXED width - neither depends on the value's magnitude.**
> **What this explains**: **why 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096 and 255 all cost exactly 55 bits** - with `gate = 1` they all take the **33-bit form**, so the total is **constant**. **It does NOT yet explain the 97-bit runs**, because those wrote the same `gate = 1` + 32 bits and should also cost 33.
> **The hypothesis for the 97-bit runs**: those two are **exactly the runs where the ps parse errored**, so **97 is where the decoder STOPPED, not a valid field cost** - the failure is **more likely downstream** in the **next-iteration prologue we pad with zeros**. **And the distinction is now concrete**: **6 (`0b110`) and 5830 have BIT 0 CLEAR**, while **255, 256, 512, 1024, 2048 and 4096 all have bit 0 SET or are single-bit values**.
> **Next**: test **7** (`0b111`) and **5** (`0b101`) - both with **bit 0 set**, close to 6. **If they parse cleanly while 6 does not, the bit-0 distinction is confirmed and it points at a downstream reader, not at the codec.**
> Acceptance: a screenshot showing the map. Evidence: [codec -97 read](evidence/experiments/20261023-codex-codec-minus97-read.json), [value class unexplained](evidence/experiments/20261023-codex-value-class-unexplained.json).
> **2026-10-23 [Value 6 costs 97 bits but 255 costs 55 - and the 97-bit runs are EXACTLY the ones where the ps parse failed]**
> Two more points: **255 -> 55 bits, `error 0`**; **6 -> 97 bits, `error 1`**.

| value | ps bits | ps error |
|---|---|---|
| **255** | **55** | **0** |
| **6** | **97** | **1** |
| 256 | 55 | 0 |
| 4096 | 55 | 0 |
| 5830 | **97** | **1** |

> **The pattern**: **the two expensive runs (6 and 5830) are exactly the two runs where the ps parse ERRORED**. In every erroring run the actors entry lands at **1405 = 1308 + 97**; in every clean run at **1363 = 1308 + 55**. **So 1405 is not a value-dependent length** - it is **simply where the decoder stopped after a failure**.
> **Why both simple theories fail**: **6 has bits 1,2 set and is SMALLER than 255, yet 255 parses fine and 6 does not**; **255 has bits 0..7 set (including 1 and 2), so "low bits set" is not the trigger either**. **The only consistent statement is: some VALUE CLASS makes the decoder fail**, and the class is **not** magnitude, bit length, parity or the low-bit pair.
> **The right next step**: **stop the value sweep** - it has produced **8 points** and the trigger is **still unexplained**. **Instead disassemble `0x6701D0` (the field codec) at the branch taken for table codec `-97` and read the exact condition** - that is **deterministic knowledge rather than another guess**.

| value | set bits | ps bits |
|---|---|---|
| 256 | bit 8 | 55 |
| 512 | bit 9 | 55 |
| 1024 | bit 10 | 55 |
| 2048 | bit 11 | 55 |
| **4096** | **bit 12** | **55** |
| 5830 | bits 1,2,6,7,8,10,12 | **97** |

| value | ps bits |

| 256 | 55 |

| **2048** | **55** |

The only point that differs is **5830**, which is **not a power of two** and whose binary form has **many set bits**.

> **2026-10-23 [Value-to-length curve, first four points: constant 55 bits up to 1024, then a 42-bit jump at 5830]**
> Measured the ps length for four values with **identical framing**:

| value | ps bits | actors error |
|---|---|---|
| 0x100 (256) | **55** | 0 |
| 0x200 (512) | **55** | 0 |
| 1024 | **55** | 0 |
| 5830 | **97** | 1 |

> **What the curve shows**: the cost is **constant at 55 bits for 256, 512 and 1024** - **three different bit lengths (9, 10, 11)** - so **the cost is not bit-length driven in that range**. At **5830** it **jumps by 42 bits**. So there is a **threshold between 1024 and 5830**, and crossing it adds a **large fixed amount (~42 bits) rather than a gradual growth**.
> **Interpretation**: a **42-bit jump looks like an extra structured field** being decoded (e.g. a second value, or a 32-bit payload plus flags), **not a length prefix**. And because 256/512/1024 are all equal, the encoder is treating those as **"small" values in a fixed slot**.
> **Next**: **bisect the threshold** - `2048` and `4096` are the natural candidates (11 and 12 bits) - then test a value **just below and just above** it to confirm the jump is a **step, not a slope**.

> Probed **`0x471C41`** (the delta path) on the `5830` body: **`delta_path = 1`**, **`delta = 1`**, `snap_trace = 1`, ps measured **97 bits**. **The `0x100` body has the same hit counts** (`delta_path = 1`, `delta = 1`).

Measuring it at **3-4 magnitudes** (`0x100`, `0x200`, `0x1000`, `5830`) gives the table, and **with that table any value can be encoded with a known length**. Each measurement is **one session**, so this is a **bounded, finite task** rather than an open-ended search.
> **Why this is the right next step**: the **framing is pinned** (55 bits for one field with a zero-ish value), **the branch is known**, and **the codec is the only variable left** - and it is a **monotone function of the value** in all likely encodings.

So the landing field is **not** the fixed "gate + 32 bits" form the `-97` codec description suggests, **at least not on this path** - the difference must come from a **variable-length component** that depends on the value's magnitude or popcount.

> **2026-10-23 [The six bits are the NEXT iteration's prologue - the post-delta region reads no bits at all]**
> Disassembled `0x471CA3..0x471D60`: it contains **no call to the bit reader** (`0x447190`). It is pure bookkeeping - the **stream-error check**, the **ring slot address** (`idiv`, `xor [ebx+0xA900],0x3613BDA3`), a **`rep movsd` of 0x16 dwords (88 bytes)** that **copies the ps struct into the history ring**, then the **clock/count increments** and the epilogue.
> **So the six bits are not read after the delta** - they can only be read by the **next loop iteration at `0x471A3E`**, i.e. `has-ps` and the header that follows it.
> **The arithmetic**: the pinned body measures **8 (header) + 40 (delta) + 6 + 1 (terminator) = 55**, and the client consumed **exactly 55**. So the next iteration's prologue costs **exactly SIX bits** before the terminating `has-ps` is consumed - which matches **`has-ps + last` (1 + 5)**.
> **Conclusion**: **there is no fixed trailer.** The block simply begins its **next iteration** (which our padding feeds as zeros) and **abandons it** when it reaches our terminator. **That is why padding moved the stop point** in the previous round.
> **Next**: to write a **second real field**, supply that next-iteration prologue explicitly (`has-ps = 1` plus its header) instead of zeros; **to write one field**, place the terminator where the client expects it - **which the pinned 55-bit body already does**.

| 0 | 49 | 65 (reads the tail) |
| 6 | **55** | **55 - exact** |

After the delta the block reads **exactly six bits** before the `has-ps` terminator, and they are **not** the hint2 radar entry (that one is gated and our padding is zeros). **Next: read `0x471CA3..0x471D60`**, the tail of the block after the delta.

| body | built | padding | measured |
|---|---|---|---|
| `idx0-v100` | 49 | 0 | **65** |
| `tr15` | 49 | 15 | **55** |

> **The insight**: with **no padding** the block consumed **65 bits = 49 of our field plus 16 bits of the hybrid tail that followed**; with **15 zeros** it stopped at **55 = 49 + 6**. **So the block keeps LOOPING after the first field and terminates on the first `has-ps` bit it reads as 0** - **which is whatever zero bit it encounters next**. **The "fixed trailer" interpretation was wrong**: there is **no fixed trailer**, there is an **under-terminated loop reading our tail**.

| `land22-v100` | 0 | 23 | 12 | 40 | **54** | 14 |

> Ran the accepted-looking body (`snapshot-single22.bin`) with the `Slot` probe at `0x471BB3`. Result: **`snap_trace` records = 0**, **slot records = 0**, and yet the client ended at **state 10**.
> **The finding**: the client reached state 10 **with ZERO calls into the snapshot parser** - `0x471980` and `0x471BB3` never fired. **So state 10 is produced by the GAMESTATE alone, not by processing a snapshot.** Therefore **every conclusion of the form "body X reaches state 10, so the snapshot was accepted" is INVALID** - **including the baseline "hybrid 167-byte body reaches state 10"** that this project has treated as ground truth since the early rounds.
> **What state 10 actually means**: most likely the client **finished the load handshake and entered the in-match network state**, with cgame alive but **no scene data** - which also explains why the frame is black. It does **NOT** mean a snapshot was parsed, validated and applied.
> **Implications**: the only reliable oracle for snapshot parsing is **breakpoint evidence** (`snap_trace` / `stream_error` at `0x4724A5`), **not the network state**. Rounds that used state 10 as an accept signal (**roughly 60-140**) **measured the wrong thing**; their **breakpoint-based** measurements remain valid **where traces exist**, and the "rejection" results that showed `stream_error = 1` were **real** rejections of the parse.
> **What to check next**: confirm that the **snapshot parser fires at all** in a run where the snapshot actually arrives (`snap_trace > 0` with the same body). **If it never fires, the snapshots may not be reaching the client at all** - which would re-contextualise the last two rounds entirely. Verify the forward/ring-bridge path **end-to-end** with the delivery assertion **plus a non-zero `snap_trace` count** before drawing any further conclusion.

> **Six shapes falsified** ((1) full header per iteration, (2) header + N records, (3) 8-bit prologue + N `[present+delta]` with `last=0`, (4) same with `last=1`, (5) 7-bit prologue + N `[present+delta]`, (6) the accepted single-field body itself, which is exactly 29 bits).
> **The emerging theory**, supported by the disassembly: **the ps block writes exactly ONE field per snapshot in this build**. After each decoded field the client runs **`add [eax+0x3BA0],1`** (the ps count) and the **loop bound is that same count**, so the bound **advances with the loop** instead of limiting it - the loop actually exits on the **`has-ps` bit**, which in our bodies arrives after one field. **And the field INDEX is not chosen by us either**: the landing index is derived from that same slot count (`esi = edx*0x58`), so **the CLIENT decides which field of the table each snapshot writes**.
> **Why this ends black-box work**: if the client picks the index, then writing "origin" is **not a matter of getting bits right - the index is out of our control**. Confirming that requires **observing the index the client picks on a real sequence**, which is a **debugger observation, not a construction experiment**. And the probe is now **validated** (`0x670FF0` calls `0x6701D0` exactly once, confirmed in the disassembly), so the failure is in the **model**, not the instrument.
> **What would settle it**: a breakpoint at **`0x471BB3`** (where the slot index is loaded) logging `[ebp-0xd0]`, `edi` and `esi` per snapshot of a real sequence; or a **captured real snapshot stream**, where the per-frame field indices are visible directly.

That count comes from the prologue's **`mode` + 5-bit `last`** (`0x471A4D`), and the accepted body had **`last = 0`** and decoded **exactly one** field. So **`last` is the field count (0 -> 1 field)** - the same convention as the cols encoder (`last_changed + 1`).

> **2026-10-23 [DECISIVE: the per-field unit is ONE `present` bit plus an optional delta - and the table really is `0xDA63E8` (24 entries)]**
> Disassembled the flag region (`0x471B9E`):
> - `0x471B9E`: `call 0x447190` -> **read ONE bit (the per-field `present` flag)**;
> - `0x471BA5`: `cmp eax,1 ; je 0x471BE7` -> **`present == 1` means SKIP this field** (no delta, no further bits);
> - `0x471BC6..0x471BC8`: `push 3, push 0xDA63E8, push 0x18, ... ; call 0x670FF0` -> **`present == 0` decodes ONE delta record**;
> - `0x471BD8` / `0x471BE1`: `game time += 1`, `ps history count += 1`;
> - `0x471BF3..0x471C00`: loop counter++, compare against the history count, loop.
> **What this establishes**: the per-field unit is **`present`(1 bit) followed, only when `present == 0`, by ONE delta record**; the delta decoder is called with the table **`0xDA63E8`** and the count **`0x18` = 24**, so **the 24-entry table at `0xDA63E8` is the correct one for this call**; and the loop iterates over the **history slot count**, not over delta records.
> **Why `rec2` failed**: it wrote `continuation = 1` right after the first delta, but **that position is the NEXT field's `present` bit**. `present == 1` means "field unchanged, skip", so the loop advanced and the rest of our bits were consumed as more present flags and deltas - **one decode, then a stream error**.
> **Corrected encoder shape**: prologue **8 bits** (`has-ps, mode, last, present`) + per field **`present(1)` and, if 0, one delta** (`continuation(1), V(5), distance, value`) + terminator (`has-ps = 0`). The accepted body: **8 + 1 + [1+5+13+1] + 1 = 29 bits** - **matches exactly**.
> **Next test**: encode **two fields** as `present(0)+delta` for field 0 and `present(0)+delta` for field 1, then the terminator. **Prediction: two decodes (indices 0 and 1) and the body stays accepted.** If that holds, **the encoder is a simple loop and multi-field - hence origin - becomes possible.**
> **Caveat recorded**: the earlier `0xDA8520` dump does **not** fit `table + 12*index` from `0xDA63E8` (8504 is not divisible by 12), so **that dump was some other structure** and the `PsField` probe's ECX should **not** be used to identify fields until that is understood.

> **2026-10-23 [Header + two records still decodes ONE field - the block has per-field flags we are not emitting]**
> Built `rec2` = prologue (8 bits) + **two delta records** (8 bits each) + terminator = **25 bits**, expecting **two** decodes. Result: **`ps_field` count = 1** (index 0 again), **`decide stream_error = 1`**, state 9.
> **What this rules out**: **"prologue once + N delta records + terminator" is NOT the layout** - the second record is not interpreted as another delta, and **only ONE `0x6701D0` call happens per snapshot** no matter how many records we write.
> **What must be true instead**: between two delta decodes the block reads **additional per-field state** we are not emitting. The disassembly of `0x471980` supports exactly that: after the delta call there is a **non-bit-reading history copy** (`0x471A8C..0x471B50`), then a **`present` bit read** (`0x471B9E` / `0x471C5C`), then the loop returns to the `has-ps` bit at `0x471CA3`. So the per-field unit is likely **[delta record] + [one or more per-field flags]**, and our second record lands in the **flag** position.
> **Honest position (round 161)**: **established** = the accepted 29-bit body decodes **exactly one field** (index 0, codec -97, value 0); the prologue is **8 bits**; a delta record is `continuation + V(5) + distance + value`; `stream_error` at `0x4724A5` is a **reliable oracle**. **Not established** = the **per-field flags between delta records**, and therefore **how to emit more than one field**, and therefore **how to write origin**.
> **Why black-box is exhausted**: **six consecutive loop-shape hypotheses have been falsified by measurement**, and the remaining space is "which extra flag bits, in what order". A **debugger breakpoint on `0x471B9E` and `0x471C5C`** would answer it in **one** session instead of dozens - and the fact that those two addresses **corrupted the parse** when we used them before is itself **evidence that they sit in the per-field flag logic**.
> **Recommendation**: **route B (debugger) is now the cheap path, not the expensive one** - the exact addresses are already known.

Combined with the disassembly of **`0x670FF0`** (continuation bit -> index -> distance -> landing field), the shape is: **ONE header, then a run of delta records, terminated by a continuation bit of 0**.
> **And the accepted body's trailing `0` bit was in fact the NEXT continuation bit (0 = no more records), not a separate "exit" flag.**
> **Corrected layout**:
> - **prologue**: `has-ps(1), mode(1), last(5), present(1)` = **8 bits**;
> - **per field**: `continuation(1), V(5), distance(...), landing value`;
> - **terminator**: a final `continuation = 0`;
> - the accepted body: **8 + [1 + 5 + 13 + 1] + 1 = 29 bits** - **matches exactly**.

> **2026-10-23 [MAJOR: reverse-reading the ACCEPTED body shows the ps block decodes exactly ONE field - and that explains everything]**
> Instead of constructing new bodies, I ran **`snapshot-single22.bin`** (the **only accepted body**, state 10) **with the `PsField` probe** and recorded every field decode. Result: **exactly ONE record** - `ecx = 0xDA8520` = **table index 0 = offset 0 / codec -97**, args `[stream, 0x11A00, 0x166244, 0, 0]`, final state **10**.
> **The model this reveals**:
> - the playerState block is a **loop**; **each iteration starts with a `has-ps` bit** and `0` terminates the block;
> - one iteration decodes **exactly one field**, and fields are decoded **in order starting at index 0** - **`V` is how many fields to reach, not which field to jump to**;
> - our accepted body wrote `has-ps=1`, `V=22`, a distance, a 1-bit zero gate, then `has-ps=0` - so the client decoded **one field (index 0, codec -97) with value 0 and exited**, which is exactly **29 bits = 14 prologue + 13 distance + 1 gate + 1 exit**;
> - that also explains the cost growth with `V` (the decoder wants more fields and consumes whatever follows) and why every "index 22" body actually wrote **the FIRST field (index 0 = offset 0 = commandTime)** - which is why they overran or crashed.
> **Consequences**: to write a real field such as origin, **all preceding fields in the `0xDA8520` table must be encoded IN ORDER**, each with its own codec. The table order is `0/-97, 1/-75, 2/-75, 3/-16, 4/-70, 5/16, 6/-88, 7/12, 8/-88, 9/12, 10/-88, 11/-88, 12/8, 13/-88, 14/-88, 15/-8, 16/-88, 17/6, 18/-87, 19/-87, 20/32, 21/-94, 22/-94, 23/-94`; the **origin-like raw floats cluster at indices 6, 8, 10, 11, 13, 14, 16**, so a coherent body needs **indices 0..16**, roughly **17 iterations**.

> **2026-10-23 [MAJOR: the field table the ps delta decoder actually uses is at `0xDA8520`, NOT `0xDA63E8`]**
> Fixed the `PsField` probe to log **ECX plus the five stack arguments**, then ran it on `snapshot-nz1.bin`. At `0x6701D0` entry: **`ecx = 0xDA8520`**, args `[0x16D9EC (stream), 0x11A00, 0x166244, 0, 0]`, and the entry read there is **`offset 0, codec -97, hint 0`**.
> **Consequences**: **every field-index/codec mapping in this project so far was built on the `0xDA63E8` table** (24 entries, offsets 76/80/84..., codecs -58/-100/...). The table the decoder is **actually indexing** starts at **`0xDA8520`** and its first entry is **offset 0 / codec -97**. So **all previous "index N -> offset X, codec Y" conclusions are invalid** - they described a **different table**. This single fact explains why the **cost model kept matching while the content never did**: the **framing arithmetic was measured correctly, but the field identities were wrong**.
> **Table at `0xDA8520`** (first 24 entries): `0/-97`, `264/-75`, `300/-75`, `704/-16`, `1384/-70`, `224/16`, `1032/-88`, `220/12`, `48/-88`, `700/12`, `56/-88`, `52/-88`, `44/8`, `64/-88`, `60/-88`, `256/-8`, `68/-88`, `716/6`, `356/-87`, `352/-87`, `12/32`, `268/-94`, `276/-94`, `284/-94`.
> **Open**: the struct behind this table is **much larger than 88 bytes** (offsets up to 1384), so it is probably the **player ENTITY state**, not the small playerstate. Also, the decoder entering at **field index 0** for our `V=22` body suggests **`V` = number of fields / last-changed + 1**, with decoding always **starting at field 0**.
> Next: **re-derive the field semantics from `0xDA8520`** and re-check the `V` semantics against it (`-97` at index 0 costs `1 + 32` bits - a plausible `commandTime`).

> **Analysis**: with `gate + 11` plain LSB bits the field costs 12 and the record should end at 40; the client stopped at **32**, i.e. it consumed only **4 bits** of the field after the gate. `0x670B3A` reads the width from `[entry + 4]`, which **is** the codec value in the `0xDA63E8` layout - so the **width rule looks right** and the **landing index** is the suspect: the record is probably **not decoding field 22**.

> **2026-10-23 [CORRECTION from the binary: the positive-width codec is a gate bit + N plain LSB-FIRST bits]**
> Read the default branch of the field codec decoder (`0x6701D0` -> **`0x670B15`**): `read 1 bit`; if **0** the value is **0** and the field ends (`mov [ebx],0`); if **1** it takes `N` from `[eax+4]` and calls **`0x66FE30` to read N bits, plain LSB-first**.
> **What was wrong**: round 116 imported the **3.3.3.3** rule ("gate bit, then `width % 8` remainder bits **first**, then whole bytes") and applied it to this build. **This build does not do that** - it reads the **plain N-bit LSB field**. That mistake gave every non-zero value we wrote the **wrong bit order**, which is consistent with **all** non-zero attempts being rejected or crashing.

> **2026-10-23 [SOLVED the ps cost model: `V` is the target POSITION and the decoder walks to it record by record]**
> Read `0x670FF0` and `0x670CB0` in full instead of guessing. **`0x670FF0`**: read 1 bit (0 -> return) -> read the index width (`5` bits for 24 fields) = **`V` = TARGET POSITION** -> read `distance` -> **copy fields `0..distance-2` without reading bits** -> decode the landing field at `distance-1` -> **loop back until the position reaches the target**. **`0x670CB0`**: `read 1 bit (1 -> distance 1)`, else `edi = 1` and `3-bit` chunks with max `7` (`while chunk == 7: edi += 7`), i.e. **`distance = 1 + sum(chunks)`**.
> **The model**: `V` is the **target position**, `distance` is the **per-record advance**. With `distance = 1` the decoder needs **one record per position step** - that is why `V=9` cost **68-70 bits** (nine records) and `V=23` cost **69**. To land on index 22 in **one** record the `distance` must be **23** (`1 + 7 + 7 + 7 + 1`), giving a predicted **~47 bits** (16 prologue + 1 continuation + 5 V + 13 distance + ~12 field) instead of **69**.
> **Why the old predictions failed**: we treated `V` as the landing field and the gap as a field-index delta, and we ported cols' **4-bit** gap coder - but this decoder uses **3-bit chunks**. Both mistakes are now fixed in code: **`write_distance` / `read_distance`** implement the 1649370 form and the self test passes (`distance` 1/2/3/8/9/23/24/100 round-trip).
> Next: encode **V=23 with distance 23** (single record, index 22, codec 11) and check the predicted ~47 bits. If confirmed, the cost model is solved and the ps block becomes **programmable**.

> **2026-10-23 [BREAKTHROUGH: the ps block is a frame loop that re-reads `has-ps` every iteration]**
> Disassembled `0x471BC8..0x471D60` and found the real control flow:
> - **`0x471A3E` = LOOP HEAD**: read 1 bit = **has-ps**; `0` -> exit (`0x471CAC`);
> - `0x471A4D`: read 1 bit = mode; mode==1 -> `last = bitpos+1`, else read **5 bits**;
> - `0x471A8C..0x471B50`: ring copy for this frame (stride `0x58`);
> - `0x471B9E`: read 1 bit = **present**; `1` -> skip; `0` -> `call 0x670FF0` (delta decoder at `0x471BC8`);
> - **`0x471CA3`**: `cmp [edi],0; je 0x471A3E` -> **loop back to the header**.
> **This explains the earlier measurements**: an all-zero body costs `1 (has-ps=1) + 1 (mode) + 5 (last) + 1 (present) + 1 (has-ps=0 -> exit) = 9-10 bits`, exactly the 10 bits measured in round 58.
> **Why encoder v0 failed**: v0 modelled one header plus a long field loop with a closing bit; in reality **every frame costs 3 header bits + 1 present bit** and the block ends when has-ps reads 0, so both the present-bit count and the tail placement were wrong.
> Next: rebuild as `[has-ps=1, mode, last] + [present=0] + delta(continuation + 5-bit index + distance + codec) + [has-ps=0] + hybrid tail`, expect the actors entry bit to match exactly, then try a real origin value.
> Acceptance: a screenshot showing the map; nothing else counts. Evidence: [ps frame loop](evidence/experiments/20261023-codex-ps-frame-loop.json).

> **2026-10-23 [ps codec fully mapped: distance reader + positive-width default branch decoded]**
> **Distance (`0x670CB0`)**: args `[8]=stream, [0xc]=bits (callers pass 3)`. If `bits==1` it is a unary run (read until a 1, return the count); otherwise read 1 bit (1 = distance 1), else read `bits` bits and accept that value unless it is `(1<<bits)-1`, otherwise continue into a longer form - an **Elias-gamma style delta index coder**.
> **Default branch (`0x670B15`)** - reached for **positive fixed widths**: `call 0x447190` reads **1 bit**; if 0 the field value is **0**; if 1 it calls `0x66FE30(field->codec)` to read `codec` bits and convert, then stores.
> **Complete ps stream layout**: `has-ps(1)` + `mode(1)` + `5-bit last` + per-field `present(1)` + delta decoder (`continuation(1)` + `5-bit index` + distance + per-field codec) + codecs (`positive N` = 1 zero-flag + N bits; `-57` = 1-bit bool; `-58/-100` = float forms).
> Next: implement the encoder in Python, first targeting a ps that carries only the three **origin** fields (indices 8/13/22, codecs 10/10/11) so the camera has a position; validate with the ps-entry/actors-entry bit cursors.
> Acceptance: a screenshot showing the map; nothing else counts. Evidence: [ps codec complete](evidence/experiments/20261023-codex-ps-codec-complete.json), [codec switch](evidence/experiments/20261023-codex-codec-switch.json).
> **2026-10-23 [Full codec switch enumerated (46 codecs); the four ps codecs decoded]**
> `0x6701D0` is a **linear if-chain over 46 codec constants** (`-64, -63, -62, -101, -102, -80, ... -58, -57, -56, -87, ...`). The ps table uses only four of them plus fixed widths:
> - **`-57`** (`0x6708E9`): `call 0x447190` = 1 bit -> `setne` -> store byte = **1-bit boolean**;
> - **`-58`** (`0x6708BF`): load float constant `[0xD599EC]` -> `call 0x66FE90` -> store = **float with fixed scale**;
> - **`-100`** (`0x6708AD` -> `0x670B5B`): load previous float `[edi]` -> `call 0x66FEE0` -> store = **float delta vs previous**;
> - **`-97`** (`0x67069C` -> `0x670BBF`, shared with `-74/-72/-70`).
> Also noted: `-73/-71` -> `0x670BA5` `call 0x66EE10` = integer read; `-101` = float angle with rounding; `-102` = float vector; codec `0` = float with a 1+1+5-bit mantissa form.
